page7_img_author_1.png.title: Author portrait headshot from the article's about-authors section
page7_img_author_1.png.description: A close-up rectangular headshot of a smiling, bespectacled adult man shown from the shoulders up, wearing a white shirt and sporting short light-brown hair and a trimmed beard. The photo is framed with a thin dark border and set against a pale-yellow background with diagonal stripes; an orange vertical bar at the left edge shows the partial white vertical label “AUTHOR.” The image appears as one of the author portraits in the magazine’s “About the Authors” section and focuses on the subject’s face and upper torso with a neutral indoor backdrop.

page7_img_author_3.png.title: Smiling male author portrait headshot with brick background
page7_img_author_3.png.description: A close-up, framed author headshot used in the article’s “About the Authors” section. The cropped photo shows a smiling adult man with short dark hair and fair skin, wearing a dark top; only part of his face and shoulder are visible. A narrow dark border surrounds the rectangular image, and a brick wall is visible in the background. The photograph is placed on a cream background with diagonal pinstripes and a solid orange vertical bar at the left edge of the page.

page3_img_1.png.title: Taxonomy of crowdsourcing tasks by emergence and contribution type
page3_img_1.png.description: A 2x2 matrix classifying crowdsourcing tasks along two dimensions: emergent versus nonemergent value (vertical) and homogeneous versus heterogeneous contributions (horizontal). The four quadrants are labeled Rating (top-left: many similar judgments aggregated — illustrated by red dots with arrows converging; example: user ratings of mobile apps), Creation (top-right: interdependent, diverse contributions combined — shown as different shapes with interconnected arrows; example: open source software), Processing (bottom-left: independent, uniform actions — parallel arrows from identical circles; example: bug reporting), and Problem solving (bottom-right: independent, diverse solutions — distinct shapes each producing a separate output arrow; example: Stack Overflow Q&A). The figure emphasizes how whether contributions are valued individually or only through combination, and whether they are qualitatively different, determines the appropriate crowdsourcing approach and typical outcomes.

page4_img_1.png.title: Table mapping development phases to crowdsourcing challenges and research
page4_img_1.png.description: A three-column table that pairs six software-development phases (Onboarding, Requirements elicitation, Development, Testing, Maintenance, and Evolution) with a key challenge for each phase and the article(s) in this issue that address it. For Onboarding, Alexandre Zanatta and colleagues examine barriers newcomers face when joining crowdsourced projects; Requirements elicitation is linked to Eduard Groen et al.’s vision for eliciting requirements from the crowd. Development cites Rabe Abdalkareem, Emad Shihab, and Juergen Rilling’s study of how developers use Stack Overflow; Testing highlights the problem of exercising apps across diverse hardware and Niklas Leicht, Ivo Blohm, and Jan Marco Leimeister’s three crowdsourced testing approaches. Maintenance notes Sahar Badihi and Abbas Heydarnoori’s CrowdSummarizer for generating code summaries, and Evolution points to María Gómez and colleagues’ App Store 2.0 architecture for incorporating large-scale user feedback.

page5_img_1.png.title: Callout: Crowdsourcing's potential to disrupt software development
page5_img_1.png.description: A full-width highlighted callout in teal type on a pale-orange background proclaims that many forms of crowdsourcing could further disrupt software development practice. The graphic is a visual emphasis in the issue’s overview, reinforcing the editors’ argument that beyond familiar examples (Stack Overflow, bug bounties, open source), additional and emerging crowdsourcing approaches deserve attention. Its prominent placement and large sans-serif typography draw the reader’s eye to the theme that diverse crowdsourcing methods can affect multiple phases of software development covered by the selected articles.

page7_img_author_2.png.title: Author headshot portrait (assistant professor)
page7_img_author_2.png.description: A color head-and-shoulders portrait photograph of an adult man with short light-brown hair and light facial stubble, facing the camera with a slight smile. He wears a blue collared shirt and is photographed against a soft, out-of-focus blue-gray background; the photo is framed with a thin dark border. The image appears in the magazine’s “About the Authors” section as the second author’s portrait, placed on a cream page with diagonal stripes and an orange vertical tab at the left. The photo visually accompanies the biographical blurb identifying this person as an assistant professor of computer science.

page1_img_1.png.title: Developer workspace connected to dispersed crowd (crowdsourcing visualization)
page1_img_1.png.description: A top-down illustration shows a person seated at a desk with a laptop and tablet beside a window; a black-and-yellow header strip at the top reads “FOCUS: GUEST EDITORS’ INTRODUCTION.” From the desk a turquoise, circuit-like schematic of lines and boxes extends through the window and down to a tiled outdoor plaza, where numerous pedestrians are circled as nodes, visually linking each individual to the workstation. Desktop items (coffee mug, stacked folders, smartphone, small printer) anchor the scene while the overlay conveys data or task flows between a single developer’s environment and many remote contributors, symbolizing crowdsourcing and distributed participation.

page7_img_multimedia_ad.png.title: Link to multimedia content for the article
page7_img_multimedia_ad.png.description: A dark-gray rectangular advertisement panel with white sans-serif text directing readers to the online multimedia page: “See www.computer.org/software-multimedia for multimedia content related to this article.” The panel includes a faint abstract circuit-like background and a cropped white graphic at the left edge. Placed in the issue as a multimedia ad, it points readers to the IEEE Computer Society web page where supplementary audio/visual or interactive resources for the article can be found.

page7_img_mycs_ad.png.title: myCS subscriptions portal advertisement banner
page7_img_mycs_ad.png.description: A dark-gray rectangular banner promoting the myCS publications portal. At left is the myCS logo (lowercase “my” and larger “CS” in pale blue), and to the right white text reads “Read your subscriptions through the myCS publications portal at” with a prominent bold URL beneath: “http://mycs.computer.org”. The design uses high-contrast white and pale-blue text on a dark background to highlight the portal URL for readers.

page7_img_call_for_articles.png.title: IEEE Software — Call for Articles advertisement
page7_img_call_for_articles.png.description: A full‑page advertisement calling for article submissions to IEEE Software, split visually into a teal left panel with a close‑up of eyeglasses and bold white text reading “Call for,” and a white right panel dominated by a large turquoise “Articles.” The right panel states the magazine’s aims — to publish practical, readable pieces for both experts and nonexperts — and gives submission constraints (original work, maximum 4,700 words, with up to 250 words allowed per table or figure). Contact and guidance information is provided (author guidelines at www.computer.org/software/author, email software@computer.org, and the magazine site www.computer.org/software), and the IEEE Software logo appears at the bottom of the left panel.
